title: Buxar Hands Over the Diwani
subtitle: When Cannons Met the Emperor’s Seal
figure: Hector Munro and Shah Alam II
era: Battle of Buxar and Treaty of Allahabad, 1764-1765 CE
moral: A battlefield can become a ledger.

sources.citation: Ghulam Hussain Khan Tabatabai, Siyar ul-Mutakhkhirin, c. 1780
sources.note: Contemporary Indian narrative of Bengal, Awadh and Company politics.

sources.citation: Hector Munro's dispatches and Fort William Council records, India Office Records
sources.note: Company-side official battlefield and administrative records.
Primary legal instrument granting the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

panels.shot: split-composition wide, half a smoky battlefield at Buxar, half a dim hall with a Mughal emperor sealing a document

dialogue.text: In 1764, at Buxar, muskets spoke; in 1765, at Allahabad, ink flowed. Between Hector Munro’s guns and Shah Alam II’s seal, a trading company quietly became a tax‑collecting power over millions.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a large wall map of eastern India lit by flickering lamplight

dialogue.text: After Plassey, Bengal did not fall in a single stroke. It tottered for years, between nawabs, bankers and a Company that still pretended to be only a trader.

panels.shot: medium wide inside a nawab’s durbar, slightly low angle to show hierarchy

dialogue.text: Mir Qasim, the new nawab of Bengal, quarrelled with the Company over duties and trade privileges. In Awadh, Shuja-ud-Daula watched uneasily. Shah Alam II, emperor without a capital, sought a path back to power.

panels.shot: dynamic oblique overhead of marching columns converging along the Ganga

dialogue.text: In 1764, their interests met in one decision: to challenge the Company in open field. The nawab of Bengal, the nawab of Awadh and the Mughal emperor formed a fragile coalition, marching towards Buxar on the Ganga.

panels.shot: low-angle medium on Munro on horseback against a hazy dawn

dialogue.text: Facing them stood Hector Munro with a much smaller force, but drilled battalions and well‑served guns. His dispatches speak of discipline, steady volleys and the quiet confidence of men used to line and file.

panels.shot: wide panoramic battlefield shot, slightly elevated, capturing both armies at the moment before engagement

dialogue.text: On 22 October 1764, near Buxar, the armies drew up. Ghulam Hussain Khan later wrote of a coalition strong in numbers but loose in command, confronting Company troops whose strength lay in cohesion more than in size.

panels.shot: tight, dramatic three-quarter view of allied guns firing, smoke rolling across

dialogue.text: Guns opened first. The coalition fielded many pieces, yet coordination faltered. Munro’s own records recount how his artillery answered methodically, each shot part of a measured pattern rather than a scattered roar.

panels.shot: medium wide on Munro and sepoys firing volleys, slight low angle to emphasize discipline

dialogue.speaker: hector_munro_and_shah_alam_ii
dialogue.text: Steady, men. Fire by platoons—hold the line.

panels.shot: wide shot of allied line beginning to waver, seen from behind their ranks

dialogue.text: As the day wore on, cohesion broke on the allied side. The Siyar ul-Mutakhkhirin remembers confusion and sudden retreats. Munro reported the opposing line giving way, their guns and camp left exposed.

panels.shot: dramatic ground-level shot of abandoned artillery and a disordered camp, with the Company in the background

dialogue.text: By evening, the coalition was routed. British records claim 133 guns taken and rich cash stores seized. However we weigh their figures, the result is clear: the nawab of Awadh and the emperor could no longer dictate terms by force.

panels.shot: intimate medium shot of Shah Alam II in a quiet tent after defeat, lantern light casting long shadows

dialogue.text: For Shah Alam II, Buxar was another bitter turn. Once emperor in name, now defeated ally, he had seen Delhi lost and now watched another hope fall at the Ganga’s edge. His path would turn from sword to seal.

panels.shot: wide view of Allahabad fort and confluence, majestic, from a distance at sunset

dialogue.text: In 1765, the road led to Allahabad, where the Yamuna meets the Ganga. There, under Company protection, the emperor set up his camp, and negotiations began that would bind Bengal’s revenue to a foreign corporation.

panels.shot: medium interior of a formal meeting hall within Allahabad fort, balanced two-shot of Munro and Shah Alam II

dialogue.speaker: hector_munro_and_shah_alam_ii
dialogue.text: Between us, Majesty, the pen must now finish what the sword began.

panels.shot: close-up on a scribe’s hands writing Persian script on thick paper, with seals and ink nearby

dialogue.text: The Treaty of Allahabad took shape in careful script. One key clause granted the English Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa—the right to collect revenue in the emperor’s name, for an annual payment to his court.

panels.shot: tight, reverent close-up of Shah Alam II’s hand pressing his seal on the document

dialogue.text: On 16 August 1765, the emperor affixed his seal. In form, he remained sovereign. In practice, he granted a private company the fiscal lifeblood of three rich provinces, in exchange for tribute and protection.

panels.shot: medium shot of Munro and Company officials examining revenue ledgers and maps, slight overhead

dialogue.text: From Fort William’s records we see what followed: surveys, new collectors, streams of coin redirected to Company treasuries. Buxar’s battlefield victory became, through Allahabad’s treaty, a steady claim upon land and labour.

panels.shot: somber medium on Shah Alam II in his Allahabad camp, gazing toward the river, profile view

dialogue.text: Ghulam Hussain Khan saw in these years an emperor forced to trade authority for survival. For Shah Alam II, the diwani grant was both necessity and loss: a way to draw revenue, but also an admission of altered power.

panels.shot: broad, time-lapse style bird’s-eye composite over Bengal’s countryside, hinting at future changes

dialogue.text: Plassey had placed a nawab under Company influence, but Buxar and Allahabad gave formal, imperial sanction to Company revenue rights. A battlefield decision rippled into the daily lives of cultivators, traders and zamindars across the delta.

panels.shot: split close-up of Munro’s weathered face fading into Shah Alam II’s lined visage, both looking in opposite directions

dialogue.text: Buxar did not end in a single victory cry; it ended in a signature that turned battle into bookkeeping. In Munro’s volleys and Shah Alam’s seal, we see how, in 1765, a ledger quietly took the place of a throne.
